Now is a time and a place for a public
hearing on agenda item 9A, a
recommendation of the public works
director that the city council adopt
separate resolutions approving the 2025
urban water management and water
shortage contingency plan in their
submittal to the Department of Water
Resources. Is there a staff
presentation?
>> Yes, Mr. Mayor. Today's presentation
will be given by Andy Darlick, water
operations manager.
Good evening, mayor and members of the
city council. Andy Darlac, water
operations manager with with the public
works department. Tonight, I will
present the city's 2025 urban water
management plan. This plan serves as the
city's long range water resource
planning document and demonstrates our
ability to reliably meet customer water
demands into the future. Next slide,
please.
California law requires urban water
suppliers serving more than 3,000
customers or delivering more than 3,000
acre feet of water annually to prepare
and update an urban water management
plan every 5 years. The plan is a
comprehensive planning document that
evaluates current and future water
supplies, projected customer demands,
water conservation efforts, drought
preparedness, and long-term reliability.
The plan also incorporates the city's
water shortage contingency plan which
outlines response actions during periods
of water supply shortages. Ultimately,
the plan demonstrates that Torrance has
a resilient and sustainable water supply
portfolio capable of meeting future
needs. Next slide, please.
For preparation of the 2025 urban water
management plan, the city retained SA
Associates, a consulting firm with
extensive experience in water resource
planning. The project included extensive
data collection, review of regulatory
requirements, analysis of water supply
and demand projections, climate
resiliency evaluations, and assessment
of future water resource needs. Staff
worked closely with the consultant
throughout the process to ensure that
operational data, capital improvement
projects, and future water supply
initiatives were accurately reflected in
the plan. Following completion of the
analysis, the draft urban water
management plan was prepared for public
review, adoption, and submittal to the
California Department of Water
Resources. Next slide, please.
This slide illustrates the city's
current water supply portfolio and
anticipated future supply mix. Today,
approximately 60% of Torrance's water
supply is imported through the
Metropolitan Water District. Local
supplies currently account for the
remaining 40% through the North Torrance
wellfield and the Goldsworthy Dalter.
Looking ahead, the city is continuing
its strategy of increasing local water
production with the addition of the
Vaness wellfield and expansion of local
groundwater resources. Importer water
reliance is projected to decrease from
approximately 60% today to about 35% in
the future. This diversification
improves reliability, enhances drought
resilience, and helps reduce dependence
on imported water supplies. Next slide,
please.
In conclusion, the urban water
management plan demonstrates that
Torrance has sufficient water supplies
to reliably meet customer demands
through at least the year 2050 under
normal single dry year and multiple
dryear conditions. The plan confirms
that the city's investments in
groundwater production, Delaw, and
future wellfield development continue to
strengthen our long-term water supply
reliability and sustainability. The
urban water management plan satisfies
all applicable state requirements and
will be submitted to the department of
water resources following council
adoption. This concludes my
presentation. Staff recommends adoption
of the resolutions approving the 2025
urban water management plan and the
water shortage contingency plan. Thank
you and staff is available for any
questions.
